overview.title: Recurrent dropout: Yarin Gal's time-constant masks and Listing 13.22
overview.subsection: 13.3.4 Using recurrent dropout to fight overfitting
overview.main_topic: Why the first LSTM model overfits, why naive dropout fails in recurrent networks, the correct scheme (the same dropout mask at every timestep, applied both to inputs and to inner recurrent activations), Keras's dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments, and the first half of Listing 13.22
overview.central_idea: Dropout in an RNN must use a temporally constant mask, both on the layer's inputs and on its recurrent activations (recurrent dropout); a mask that changes every timestep disrupts the error signal propagated through time. Keras exposes this through the dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments, and with that regularization the LSTM can be made twice as wide and trained five times longer.
overview.importance: This is the book's treatment of the standard way to regularize LSTM/GRU layers. It is the first improvement applied to the baseline-beating LSTM and yields the result on p.398 (validation MAE 2.27). The two arguments, dropout and recurrent_dropout, are used again in the stacked GRU and bidirectional models that follow.
learning_objectives: Diagnose overfitting from diverging training and validation losses.
Explain why applying a regular dropout layer before a recurrent layer hinders learning.
State Gal's rule: use the same dropout mask at every timestep, for inputs and for recurrent activations.
Distinguish the dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments of Keras recurrent layers.
Explain the two design changes made alongside recurrent dropout in Listing 13.22: twice as many units and five times as many epochs.
Read the first half of Listing 13.22 and say what each line does.
prerequisites: The LSTM model of Listing 13.12 (LSTM(16), 10 epochs; p.388)
Backpropagation through time: gradients flow backward across timesteps (p.389-393)

summary:
**The problem.** Finishing the sentence from p.396: the training and validation curves of the first LSTM model (Listing 13.12, `LSTM(16)`, p.388) show that it overfits quickly despite having very few units; the training and validation losses diverge considerably after a few epochs. The classic remedy is **dropout**, which randomly zeros out input units of a layer to break happenstance correlations in the training data. But applying dropout correctly in recurrent networks 'isn't a trivial question'.

**The answer (Yarin Gal).** It has long been known that applying dropout *before* a recurrent layer hinders learning rather than regularizing. In 2015, as part of his PhD thesis on Bayesian deep learning (footnote 5), Yarin Gal determined the proper way:

1. Apply **the same dropout mask** (the same pattern of dropped units) at every timestep, instead of a mask that varies randomly from timestep to timestep.
2. To regularize the representations formed by the recurrent gates of layers like `GRU` and `LSTM`, also apply a temporally constant mask to the **inner recurrent activations** of the layer: a *recurrent dropout mask*.

A constant mask lets the network properly propagate its learning error through time; a temporally random mask would disrupt this error signal.

**In Keras.** Gal did his research with Keras and helped build the mechanism into its recurrent layers. Every Keras recurrent layer has two arguments: `dropout` (rate for the layer's input units) and `recurrent_dropout` (rate for the recurrent units).

**The experiment.** Dropout means less reliance on small network size for regularization, so the `LSTM` gets **twice as many units** (32 instead of 16); without dropout this network would overfit right away. Dropout-regularized networks take longer to converge, so training runs for **five times as many epochs** (50 instead of 10). Listing 13.22 builds `LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25)`, followed by `Dropout(0.5)` to regularize the `Dense(1)` output layer, and a `ModelCheckpoint` callback saving the best model to `jena_lstm_dropout.keras`. Compilation and training continue on p.398.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The first LSTM model's training and validation curves show it overfits quickly, even with very few units: the two losses diverge considerably after a few epochs. Small capacity was implicitly acting as the regularizer, and it was not enough. The authors now want an explicit regularizer so the network can be made bigger without overfitting.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Divergence between training and validation loss is the standard overfitting signal (chapter 5). Recognizing it is what justifies the rest of this subsection.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'happenstance correlations' are what Hinton calls conspiracies (p.192); the noise injected by dropout prevents units from co-adapting to fit those coincidences.

Randomly setting a fraction of a layer's units to zero during training (p.191).

paragraphs.excerpt: It has long been known that applying dropout before a recurrent layer hinders
paragraphs.what_it_says: Applying dropout before a recurrent layer has long been known to hinder learning. In 2015, Yarin Gal, in his PhD work on Bayesian deep learning, determined the proper method: apply the same dropout mask at every timestep instead of one that varies randomly over time. Moreover, to regularize the representations formed by the recurrent gates of GRU and LSTM, a temporally constant mask should be applied to the inner recurrent activations (a recurrent dropout mask). A constant mask lets the network propagate its learning error through time; a temporally random mask would disrupt this error signal and harm learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There are two places to drop units in an RNN: the input x_t fed into the cell at each step, and the state h_{t-1} fed back into the cell. Gal's prescription samples one mask for each per sequence and reuses it across all timesteps. Dropping different recurrent units at each step injects fresh noise into the state at every step; over 120 timesteps that noise compounds and drowns the signal the network is trying to carry, and the gradient flowing back through time sees a different random network at each step.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is why you should not just add a Dropout layer in front of an LSTM and expect it to help; use the layer's own arguments instead.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in Gal and Ghahramani's variational interpretation, sampling one mask per sequence corresponds to sampling one set of weights from an approximate posterior and using it for the whole sequence, which is consistent with the RNN's weight sharing across time. Per-timestep masks would correspond to different weights at each step, breaking that sharing.

terminology.meaning: The binary pattern of which units are kept (1) and which are dropped (0).
A mask sampled once per sequence and reused at every timestep.
A temporally constant mask applied to the recurrent activations (the state fed back into the cell).
Treating network weights as uncertain (probability distributions); Gal showed dropout can be interpreted as approximate Bayesian inference.

paragraphs.excerpt: Yarin Gal did his research using Keras and helped build this mechanism directly
paragraphs.what_it_says: Gal used Keras for his research and helped build the mechanism into Keras recurrent layers. Every recurrent layer has two dropout-related arguments: dropout, the dropout rate for the layer's input units, and recurrent_dropout, the rate for the recurrent units. The plan is to add recurrent dropout to the LSTM layer of the first LSTM example and see how it affects overfitting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two arguments map exactly onto the two masks of the previous paragraph: dropout masks x_t, recurrent_dropout masks the state fed back into the cell. Both are temporally constant inside the layer, so you get Gal's scheme for free.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the practical API. Listing 13.22 uses only recurrent_dropout; later models (stacked GRU on p.399-400) use the same arguments.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: dropout and recurrent_dropout are active only in training; at inference the layer runs deterministically. On GPU, recurrent_dropout > 0 prevents use of the cuDNN kernel, which the sidebar on p.398-399 discusses.

terminology.meaning: Float rate for dropping the input units of a Keras recurrent layer.
Float rate for dropping the recurrent units of a Keras recurrent layer.

p.399: stacked recurrent layers regularized with dropout.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Because dropout handles regularization, the network does not need to be kept small; the LSTM gets twice as many units, which should be more expressive (without dropout this network would overfit right away, try it). Dropout-regularized networks take much longer to converge, so training runs for five times as many epochs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Concretely: LSTM(16) becomes LSTM(32), and epochs=10 (p.388) becomes epochs=50 (p.398). This is the general pattern of regularization: replace an implicit regularizer (low capacity) with an explicit one (dropout) so that capacity can be increased.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains two otherwise unexplained numbers in Listing 13.22, and it shows that regularization techniques interact with capacity and training time.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Why dropout slows convergence (beyond the book): each step's gradient is computed on a randomly thinned network, so gradient estimates are noisier, and the network must learn redundant representations robust to missing units.

terminology.meaning: The point in training where loss stops improving meaningfully.

concepts.name: Recurrent dropout
concepts.definition: Dropout applied with a temporally constant mask to the inner recurrent activations of a recurrent layer; exposed as recurrent_dropout in Keras.
concepts.intuition: For a whole sequence, the same memory units are switched off at every step, so the network cannot rely on any one of them, yet the signal passed through time stays consistent.
concepts.technical: One Bernoulli mask m_h is sampled per sequence (and per training step) and applied elementwise to h_{t-1} before it enters the cell's recurrent transformations at all timesteps.
concepts.significance: The page's prescribed way to regularize GRU and LSTM recurrent representations; Listing 13.22 uses recurrent_dropout=0.25.
concepts.misconception: That a per-timestep random mask is 'more random and therefore better regularization'; the page says it disrupts the error signal and harms learning.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.definition: Randomly zeroing out a fraction of a layer's units during training to break happenstance correlations in the training data.
concepts.intuition: No unit can count on any particular partner being present, so units must be individually useful.
concepts.technical: In Keras, the Dropout layer applies to the output of the previous layer; layers.Dropout(0.5) here drops half of the 32 LSTM outputs before the Dense layer.
concepts.significance: The classic overfitting remedy (p.191), here used in two forms: inside the LSTM (recurrent) and as a regular layer after it.
concepts.misconception: That dropout is active at inference time; it only operates during training.

concepts.name: Temporally constant dropout mask
concepts.definition: A dropout mask sampled once and reused at every timestep of a sequence.
concepts.intuition: Like covering the same keys of a piano for an entire song rather than different keys for each note.
concepts.technical: Applies to both the inputs (Keras dropout argument) and the recurrent state (recurrent_dropout argument).
concepts.significance: Gal's key insight: it lets the error propagate properly through time.
concepts.example: With 6 units and mask [1,0,1,1,0,1], units 2 and 5 are zero at t=1, 2, ..., 120.
concepts.misconception: That a constant mask means the same units are dropped for the entire training run; a new mask is sampled for each sequence/batch, but held fixed across that sequence's timesteps.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: The model fits training data specifics so that validation performance stops improving while training performance keeps improving.
concepts.intuition: Memorizing the answers to practice questions instead of learning the subject.
concepts.technical: Seen here as training and validation losses diverging after a few epochs for the LSTM(16) model.
concepts.example: The first LSTM reached val MAE 2.39 but its curves diverge early (p.388, p.397).
concepts.misconception: That small models cannot overfit; the page notes this one overfits 'despite only having very few units'.

math.title: Recurrent layer with time-constant input and recurrent dropout masks
math.latex: h_t = \phi\big(W\,(m_x \odot x_t) + U\,(m_h \odot h_{t-1}) + b\big),\qquad m_x \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p_x),\ m_h \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p_h)\ \text{sampled once per sequence}
math.source_text: Described in words: 'the same dropout mask ... should be applied at every timestep' and 'a temporally constant dropout mask should be applied to the inner recurrent activations of the layer'

variables.meaning: Input vector at timestep t (14 weather features in the Jena task).
Recurrent state from the previous timestep.
Input dropout mask (Keras dropout argument, rate p_x), the same for all t.
Recurrent dropout mask (Keras recurrent_dropout argument, rate p_h), the same for all t.
Input weights, recurrent weights and bias (as in the SimpleRNN form on p.395).

math.operations: Elementwise masking of the input and the previous state, then the usual recurrent affine transformation and activation. In an LSTM, the same masks are applied in each of its gate transformations.
math.purpose: Formalizes Gal's prescription described in prose on the page. Note that the masks carry no t subscript: that is the whole point.
math.interpretation: Contrast with the harmful scheme, where m_x and m_h would be m_{x,t} and m_{h,t}, resampled at every step.
math.intuition: The network sees a consistently thinned version of itself for the whole sequence, so the gradient through time is computed for one coherent sub-network.
math.numerical_example: With recurrent_dropout=0.25 and 32 units, about 8 recurrent units are zeroed for an entire 120-step sequence. In Keras the kept units are also scaled by $1/(1-0.25)\approx 1.33$ during training (inverted dropout), so no rescaling is needed at inference. The scaling detail is not on this page.

code.title: Training and evaluating a dropout-regularized LSTM (model and callbacks; continues on p.398)
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))
x = layers.LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25)(inputs)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(
        "jena_lstm_dropout.keras", save_best_only=True
    )
]
code.what_it_does: Defines a Functional-API model: sequences of shape (sequence_length, num_features) go through an LSTM with 32 units and recurrent dropout 0.25, which returns only its last output; a Dropout(0.5) layer regularizes the input to the final Dense(1) regression head. A ModelCheckpoint callback saves the model with the best validation loss to jena_lstm_dropout.keras. The compile/fit lines (Adam, MSE loss, MAE metric, epochs=50) are on p.398.

line_explanations.explanation: Input of shape (120, 14): sequence_length = 120 hourly timesteps (p.382) and raw_data.shape[-1] = 14 weather features.

LSTM with twice the units of Listing 13.12 (32 vs 16) and recurrent_dropout=0.25: a time-constant mask drops 25% of the recurrent units. return_sequences is False by default, so the output is (batch, 32).

Regular Dropout on the LSTM's final output; per the callout, 'To regularize the Dense layer, we also add a Dropout layer after the LSTM.' Placing dropout after (not before) the recurrent layer is fine.
A single linear unit predicts the temperature 24 hours ahead (regression, no activation); the Model ties inputs to outputs.
ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True keeps the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss, so the best epoch can be reloaded even if later epochs overfit.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: batches of shape (batch_size, 120, 14) from train_dataset/val_dataset. Output: (batch_size, 1) temperature predictions. Side effect: jena_lstm_dropout.keras saved to disk during training.
code.algorithm: Standard supervised regression with an LSTM encoder; regularization from recurrent dropout inside the LSTM and output dropout before the head.
code.theory_link: Implements Gal's time-constant recurrent dropout described in the paragraphs above, and the 'bigger network plus explicit regularization' trade-off.

parameters.name: 32 (LSTM units)
parameters.role: Width of the LSTM state and carry; doubled from 16 because dropout now provides regularization.

pitfalls: Adding layers.Dropout before the LSTM instead of using its dropout argument: the page says dropout before a recurrent layer hinders learning.
On GPU, recurrent_dropout > 0 disables the fast cuDNN kernel and can slow training by 2-5x (sidebar, p.398-399).
Keeping epochs=10 from Listing 13.12: dropout-regularized models converge much more slowly; the book uses 50.

# AI-written: parameter count of the model and how to also drop inputs
from keras import layers
import keras

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(120, 14))
x = layers.LSTM(32, dropout=0.1, recurrent_dropout=0.25)(inputs)  # input + recurrent masks
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.summary()

deeper.title: Why a per-timestep random mask hurts
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, an intuition for the page's claim that a temporally random mask 'would disrupt this error signal'.

1. The state $h_t$ is the RNN's only memory. With a new recurrent mask each step, a unit holding useful information at step $t$ may be zeroed at step $t+1$, erasing it from the state.
2. Over 120 steps, the chance a given unit survives every step at rate 0.25 is $0.75^{120}\approx 10^{-15}$: effectively nothing can be carried through.
3. With a constant mask, each unit is either dropped for the whole sequence (probability 0.25) or kept for the whole sequence (0.75). Kept units can carry information as far as they need.
4. Backpropagation through time sees one consistent sub-network, so the gradient is that of a real (thinned) RNN rather than of a different network at every step.

deeper.title: Two masks, two places
deeper.body:
| Keras argument | What it masks | Mask over time |
|---|---|---|
| `dropout` | input units $x_t$ entering the cell | constant |
| `recurrent_dropout` | recurrent units $h_{t-1}$ fed back into the cell | constant |
| separate `layers.Dropout` after the RNN (as in Listing 13.22) | the layer's output vector | n/a when return_sequences=False (one vector per sequence) |

The first two rows are stated on this page; 'constant' for the input mask follows from 'the same dropout mask ... should be applied at every timestep'.

deeper.title: Analogy: a choir with absent singers
deeper.body: Picture a choir singing a long piece, where each singer passes the melody along. Constant dropout: some singers are absent for the whole performance, so the others learn to cover their parts and the melody stays coherent. Per-step dropout: at every bar, a random quarter of the singers fall silent and come back, so the melody keeps breaking and nobody can learn how their part connects to the next bar.

misconceptions.claim: Putting a Dropout layer right before an LSTM is the right way to regularize it.
misconceptions.correction: The page states that applying dropout before a recurrent layer hinders learning; use the layer's dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments, which apply time-constant masks.

misconceptions.claim: Resampling the dropout mask at each timestep gives stronger, better regularization.
misconceptions.correction: A temporally random mask disrupts the error signal propagated through time and harms learning.

misconceptions.claim: dropout and recurrent_dropout are two names for the same thing.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the proper way to use dropout in a recurrent network?
options: Insert a Dropout layer before the recurrent layer
Sample a new dropout mask at every timestep
Apply the same dropout mask at every timestep, including a constant mask on the recurrent activations
Apply dropout only at inference time
questions.answer: Apply the same dropout mask at every timestep, including a constant mask on the recurrent activations
questions.explanation: This is Gal's prescription. Dropout before the recurrent layer hinders learning; a per-timestep mask disrupts the error signal; dropout is a training-time technique.

questions.question: What is the difference between the dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments of a Keras recurrent layer?
questions.answer: dropout is the dropout rate for the layer's input units; recurrent_dropout is the dropout rate for its recurrent units.
questions.explanation: Both are stated on the page; together they implement the two time-constant masks of Gal's method.

questions.question: Why does a temporally random dropout mask harm learning in an RNN?
questions.answer: Because it disrupts the error signal that the network propagates through time; a constant mask lets the network properly propagate its learning error across timesteps.
questions.explanation: With a changing mask, information held in a unit can be erased at any step and the gradient is computed through a different sub-network at each step. With a constant mask the network is a consistent thinned RNN.

questions.question: Compared with the first LSTM model (Listing 13.12), what two other changes accompany recurrent dropout in Listing 13.22?
options: Half the units and twice the epochs
Twice the units and five times the epochs
The same units and ten times the epochs
A GRU instead of an LSTM and the same epochs
questions.answer: Twice the units and five times the epochs
questions.explanation: LSTM(16) becomes LSTM(32) because dropout now provides regularization, and 10 epochs become 50 because dropout-regularized networks take much longer to converge.

questions.question: The LSTM in Listing 13.22 has 32 units and receives 14 input features. Using the LSTM structure of four transformations, each with W (input x units), U (units x units) and b (units), how many trainable parameters does the LSTM layer have?
questions.explanation: The four transformations (output, i, f, k on p.395) each have their own input matrix, recurrent matrix and bias. (The book's pseudocode also has a Vo term for the carry in the output; Keras's standard LSTM does not include it, which gives 6016.)

questions.question: Why can the authors afford to double the LSTM's units once dropout is added, when the 16-unit model was already overfitting?
questions.answer: Dropout provides explicit regularization, so they no longer need to rely on small network size to limit overfitting; a larger network is more expressive. Without dropout, the 32-unit network would overfit right away.
questions.explanation: The page states this reasoning in its last paragraph: 'we won't need to rely as much on network size for regularization'.

questions.question: Could you sketch, for 4 timesteps and 6 recurrent units, what a recurrent dropout mask looks like, and contrast it with the harmful alternative?
questions.answer: Correct: the same columns are zeroed in every row (timestep). Harmful: different random columns are zeroed in each row.
